source.title: Evaluating the learnability of single-cell large language models on multiple tasks
source.authors: Yuhai Yan; Xu-Tao Wang; Dong-Yuan Song

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study's own results on single-cell foundation models challenge a general bigger-is-better expectation, reporting task-dependent effects and non-monotonic or detrimental results as model depth increases. It does not test language-model cross-entropy scaling laws directly.
record.gate_note: Rows record downstream performance under pretraining-data and model-depth variations, which bears on V6. The paper does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, so V1–V4 and V7 are not tested. It studies single-cell models but does not test whether a power-law form holds in another modality or training regime, so V5 is also not tested. Synthetic-data comparisons and representative perturbation plots are not rows here because they do not vary model or pretraining scale for V6; cited findings from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study sets out to test whether scaling laws hold for single-cell foundation models, which it calls single-cell LLMs. It varies pretraining data (full, 1%, 0.1%, none) and transformer depth, and reports downstream perturbation and annotation performance. That makes it a new-setting test of V6's direction of effect (does downstream performance improve with scale), not of any loss power law. Caveat: the subjects are gene-token transformers, not text language models, so V6's system match is approximate.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that large-scale pretraining helps cell type annotation substantially but helps perturbation prediction little. They find that increasing model size gives minimal or negative returns, which they attribute to overfitting when pretraining is absent. From synthetic-data tests they conclude that the tested scFMs mainly capture low-order statistics in perturbation prediction. They call for biologically informed, task-specific models rather than pure scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates downstream single-cell tasks by varying pretraining-data amounts and transformer depth; it does not use language-model held-out cross-entropy sweeps, power-law fits, or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome changes with task and model: pretraining benefits annotation more clearly than perturbation prediction, and model-depth trends differ across tasks and models.
record.peer_reviewed: BMC Genomics; the text states a version of record was published June 5th, 2026.
record.problems: The text gives mostly qualitative summaries and approximate values for the scale comparisons; exact results are not available in the provided text for the plotted conditions. Perturbation results report standard errors across five replicates, but numerical error bars are not stated here. The evidence concerns single-cell downstream metrics, not language-model pretraining loss or fitted scaling laws.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. Synthetic-data comparisons and representative perturbation examples were omitted because they do not report outcomes against the scale variables relevant to V6; figures are supplied as captions without underlying plotted values in the text.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss or power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
Depth is varied with width fixed, so parameter count changes too. Shape at fixed parameter count is not tested, and loss is not measured.
Single-cell modality, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.

Only direction and monotonicity are tested. There is no quantitative predictive mapping, pretraining loss is not used as a predictor, and text LLMs are not studied. Scale ranges are narrow: three data levels and depths of 1 to 20 layers.
No fitted exponents or comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Depth sweep with 1% pretraining, summarised over all configurations. For annotation, Geneformer scaled with both data and model size, while scGPT's best configuration was 6 layers with minimal pretraining. For perturbation, the best models were often small (1–6 layers) with little or no pretraining.

record.verdict_notes: The subjects are single-cell transformers over gene tokens; the paper calls them single-cell LLMs. The V6 link is therefore a cross-domain reading and is weaker than for text LMs. Scale ranges are small, and depth changes are made without retuning other dimensions. Values are mostly qualitative, read from figures. The caption and text disagree on whether the smallest subsample is 0.01% or 0.1%.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law relation in parameter count, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run power-law fits or extrapolation to larger runs are reported.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or compute-optimal parameter/token split is reported.
The paper varies transformer depth, but does not test how architecture details affect loss at fixed parameter count.
The study uses single-cell models, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in that modality or regime.

Tests downstream performance against pretraining-data availability and transformer depth in two single-cell models; does not test language models, held-out pretraining loss as a predictor, or a quantitative predictive mapping.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, or systematic comparisons of fitting choices are reported.

relationships.condition: Increasing pretraining data: Geneformer on both tasks, scGPT on cell type annotation
relationships.reason: Geneformer shows a dose-response on perturbation (R1–R3). Full pretraining lifts Geneformer annotation F1 from about 0.6 to over 0.8 (R8), and scGPT annotation also improves (R11).
relationships.display_finding: Geneformer perturbation performance improved with more data, full pretraining raised annotation F1 from about 0.6 to over 0.8, and scGPT annotation also improved.

relation.reason: Its own pretraining-data and depth sweeps directly test downstream improvement with scale under V6.

tranche.reason: The study explicitly re-examines scaling assumptions and reports absent or reversed downstream gains, requiring qualification of V6. Its central result is a challenge to scaling, beyond introducing a new setting.

source_check.notes:
The supplied text is a preprint linked to the published DOI; captions state 0.01% where narrative and Methods state 0.1%. Subsamples are cell-type-balanced from a blood/primary-tissue census subset, so comparisons also change data composition.
§2.3 adds an unrecorded interaction: minimally pretrained 6-layer scGPT gives the best annotation configuration, whereas fully pretrained large Geneformer performs best; no quantitative power-law fit or extrapolation is tested.

statements.correction: scGPT perturbation performance nearly flat across pretraining amounts (§2.1.1; R4–R7); scratch-trained annotation Macro F1 decreases with depth for both models (§2.2.2; R16–R17).
statements.problem: The study-specific claims are correct, but cited R9 and R12 concern minimal pretraining rather than annotation depth; the depth evidence is R16 and R17.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Full-data pretraining for cell type annotation, both tested models
reader_labels.reason: Both models improved with full pretraining; Geneformer rose from around 0.6 for no pretraining to over 0.8, and scGPT also showed a substantial improvement (R8, R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Pretraining-data changes for perturbation prediction and minimal pretraining for annotation
reader_labels.reason: Pretraining benefits varied by task and model: Geneformer improved with more pretraining on perturbation prediction, scGPT was nearly flat there, and minimal pretraining gave only marginal annotation gains (R1-R6, R9-R10, R12-R13).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Increasing transformer depth in the reported unpretrained model-size sweeps
reader_labels.reason: Larger depths did not consistently improve downstream performance: perturbation performance peaked at 6 layers and then declined or was no better at the largest sizes, while annotation F1 declined as depth increased (R14-R17).
